kinetren
Docs

User guide

What's new

The program shows the section of its own version in the welcome window. One section per month, newest first.

kt26.11

  • Six new shapes and plates. Edit › Create a generator › Shapes now has Polygon, Star, Arrow, Border frame, Lower-third plate (a bar with an accent stripe, which can slide in with a curve on its Reveal) and Progress bar (fills by itself over the time you set). They are drawn over whatever is on the tracks below, with smooth edges, and every colour has the eyedropper and its own transparency.
  • Four moving backgrounds. Edit › Create a generator › Background now has Moving gradient (soft blobs of three colours drifting into each other), Plasma, Particles (soft glowing dots floating up) and Pattern (stripes, dots, a grid or waves, drifting at an angle). They move by themselves — no keyframes — at the speed you set, and their colours can be taken with the eyedropper.
  • A title can be a timecode, a stopwatch or a countdown. In a Text generator's window, the new Text row chooses Typed, Timecode, Stopwatch or Countdown. A stopwatch counts up from its start, a countdown counts down to zero and stays there, in the format you pick (1:05, 1:05.3, 0:01:05 or 65.3), and a timecode runs at its frame rate. It is a title like any other: font, size, colours, outline, shadow, backing and animation all work on it. Write {} in the text to put the value inside words, like "Round ends in {}".
  • VHS Tape and Camera ISP on a whole video track now sound. Put the tape or the camera on a video track and its sound is played by that track's audio track — the one with the same number, or the one you pick in the track window's "Device sound" row. The track window shows both tracks' effects in one graph, the device's sound half right under its picture half, with its own switch.
  • Two new technical generators: Sync flash and Safe areas. Edit › Create a generator › Signal check › Sync flash puts a white flash at the start of every second (or the interval you set) with a beep on the same frame, and a bar between flashes that shows the next one coming — a clapper for checking that picture and sound line up. Safe areas draws the action-safe and title-safe frames, a centre cross and, if you want, the rule of thirds and the 4:3 cut, over whatever is on the tracks below; mute its track when you do not want it in the render.
  • Rendering spends less processor time. The picture of every frame is turned into the video's own colour format by the graphics card, the same way on every machine, and only that smaller picture travels back to the processor; the slow moments the program keeps on disk are prepared the same way.
  • Right-click menus make the thing, the window picks its kind. Right-click a track and choose Create a generator: a solid colour (a tone on an audio track) appears where you clicked and its window opens, where the pictures of all the kinds are. Right-click an event and choose Transition with next or previous: a dissolve is made and its window opens with the same kind pictures. No more long lists of kinds in those menus.
  • A double click right after another click stays a double click. On a busy machine, double-clicking an event soon after clicking somewhere else — the effects window's Done, another event — could be taken for a triple click: the effects window did not open, a region was set over the event and the cursor jumped to its start. Now three clicks count as a triple only when they are one gesture on one place, everywhere in the program.
  • Parts of the preview saved to disk play back on the graphics card. The slow moments the program prepares on its own and keeps on disk are now read by your graphics card's video decoder, not by the processor; where the computer has none, the processor still reads them.
  • See the picture after any effect. In an effect graph, Ctrl+Shift+click an effect (or right click it → "Show the picture after this effect"): the preview shows the event as it looks right after that effect, with a "Viewer" label, and a sound effect is heard up to that point. Esc, Play, or closing the window brings the full picture back. Nothing in your project changes.
  • A video event and its sound are one effect graph. Double click an event that has its linked audio: the effects window shows both chains in one graph, the picture's effects on top and the sound's below, each with its own switch. VHS Tape, Datamosh or Camera ISP stand there as one device with the sound half right under the picture half; switch the sound half off to keep the effect on the picture only, or remove the device with one cross from both.
  • The effect graph answers your keys. With the mouse over an effect graph, Delete removes the selected effect, the mute key switches it off and on, and the zoom keys show the full nodes, the small chips or the whole graph — your own key bindings, not new ones; the timeline under the window does not react to them then.
  • The effects window shows what else changes the event. After the event's own effects its graph now shows, in the order they apply, a box for each morpher layer over it and one for its track's effects — with the track that ducks it, when it has one. Double click a box to open that layer's or that track's window. The track window draws the ducking key as a box wired into its compressor. The effects of an audio event or an audio track show as nodes again; they were missing from the graph.
  • An effect's centre is set on the preview. With Radial Blur selected in an effect's window, a crosshair stands on the picture at its centre: drag it where the rays should spread from, and the Center X and Y fields follow (with a curve on the centre, the key at the playhead moves). Center X and Y now stand side by side on one row, as every X/Y pair of an effect's parameters does.
  • Closing a project that is still catching up ends sooner. If the program was still working out the picture you stopped on, the small picture it makes for the start window kept going after you closed, and the program waited for it up to its limit. Now that picture is given up after a few seconds and the program ends at once.
  • Colours can be taken from the screen with an eyedropper. Every colour in the program now has a pipette button beside it — the Greenscreen's key first, and the tints, lines and duotone of effects, a transition's colour, a title's and a generator's colours. Press it, then click the colour anywhere in the program: the preview's picture, a thumbnail, another window. The Greenscreen's green comes straight from your own frame, and the click does nothing else (it does not start playback). Esc puts the eyedropper down.
  • Saving a project with a Datamosh no longer keeps the computer busy afterwards. After Ctrl+S the program makes the small picture of the project you see in the start window; it used to work that frame out again from nothing, which for a Datamosh meant its whole broken stream — some twenty seconds on a computer without a graphics card. It now takes the frame the preview already shows.
  • Effect chains are now a small node graph. In the effects window, the morpher window and the track window the row of effect names is replaced by nodes joined by wires, laid out in the order the effects run: in a morpher the picture's effects on one line and the sound's under it, and VHS Tape, Datamosh or Camera ISP stand as one device with the picture half over the sound half. Each node has its switch and its cross and shows two or three of its main sliders — Camera ISP's exposure, gain and sharpening — while its whole panel stays below. Drag a node onto another to change the order; a long chain shrinks to small chips so it always fits, Ctrl+wheel over the graph shows the full nodes, and "Frame all" brings the whole graph back.
  • A file dragged from the media bin lands where you aimed. Scrub a video's card to the moment you want, press there and drag the card to a track: the whole file lands with that moment under the mouse. Hold Alt over the track to put the file's start under the mouse instead, Alt+Shift for its end — you can press or let go of them right up to the drop. Before you let go, the green outline on the track is the file itself, as long as it will be and where it will stand, and the status line says which point lands under the mouse.
  • Markers carry notes. Right-click a marker's flag and choose Note…: a field opens right at the flag where you can write as much as you like, on several lines (Enter starts a new line; a click elsewhere keeps the text, Esc leaves the note as it was). A marker with a note shows a small note sign after its name, and pointing at the flag reads the note in the status line. The note is separate from the marker's name, so names stay short. Notes go out to OpenTimelineIO as marker comments, and comments in a file you import become notes.
  • Several keys of a curve can be selected and moved together. In an effect's (or a camera's, a transition's, a generator's, a mask's) curve graph, the keys at both ends of the segments you select are selected too — they turn white. Shift+click a key to add it to the selection or take it out, and Shift+drag over empty space to add more segments. Drag any white key and all of them move: by the same time, the dragged one landing on a frame, and by the same height, each staying in its parameter's range. The block stops before a key that is not selected, and the whole move is one undo step. Pulling a key up past the top of the graph no longer jumps the playhead instead.
  • Copying part of a selected event works. With one event selected, a region drawn over part of it used to copy the whole event; now Copy takes just that event's part under the region (and its linked audio), and nothing of the other events the region crosses. A region elsewhere, or one that covers the whole event, still copies the whole event.
  • Choosing a transition or a generator now shows pictures, as choosing an effect does. The Kind field of a transition's window opens a gallery: every kind is a small picture of your own cut with that transition halfway through, grouped by family. The Kind field of a generator's window shows every kind as it would look on that event. Click a picture to pick it. The pictures appear about a second after the window opens, as the effect pictures do.
  • A morpher layer's VHS Tape, Datamosh or Camera ISP can leave the sound alone. Such an effect works on the picture and the sound at once, and in a morpher layer its sound half was added out of sight, with no way to switch it off. The layer's effect chain now shows the sound half next to the picture half, marked with a speaker, and its checkbox switches the device's sound off for that layer while the picture keeps the effect; switching the picture half off likewise keeps the sound. Layers in projects saved before keep sounding as they did until you switch the sound off.
  • C cuts out the region. Draw a region with I and O and press C: the part of every event inside it is gone and the rest stays where it was, in one undo step. The same is in the Edit menu as "Cut out the region interior"; before, it was only in the right-click menu of an empty spot on a track. Without a region, C says to draw one first.
  • "Marker over the region" always makes a new marker. Right-clicking the region's edge used to sometimes stretch a marker that already stood at the region's start instead of making a new one. Now that is a separate item, "Stretch the marker over the region", shown only when there is such a marker; "Marker over the region" never changes an existing marker, and says which item to use when one is in the way. The M key works as before.
  • Datamosh can break at a small size and still be sharp. At an encoded height of 144 lines the break has its coarse, chunky look, but the picture was the codec's tiny picture stretched over your frame. A Datamosh you add from now on is Sharp, and a project you saved before keeps its look (untick Sharp in the effect's window for the soft picture): the codec still decides the break at its own size — the same blocks, the same motion, the same dropped keyframes — and the picture is carried at your project's resolution, with your footage's detail; an intact stretch is your footage exactly. The sound of the broken stream is unchanged. Datamosh's work in the preview now also follows the preview's size: what goes in front of it (Camera ISP, VHS Tape) runs at the preview's size instead of the codec's when the codec is larger, so a loop with it catches up sooner; the render keeps your full settings.
  • A slow part you played plays smoothly the next time, even after a restart. When a part of the timeline is too heavy for your computer to draw while it plays — VHS Tape, Camera ISP, Datamosh, several layers at once — the program now finishes its frames by itself once you stop and leave the mouse for a moment and keeps them on disk as video compressed by your graphics card's encoder, like a prerender in VEGAS. The next time that part plays, the frames come from the disk with nothing to draw again, from the first lap and after you reopen the project too. It only does this for frames it measured too slow for real time, it stops the moment you touch the mouse or the keyboard, press Play or start a render, and the disk it takes is capped at 2 GB, the oldest frames going first. On a computer whose graphics card has no video encoder the program does not do this (the processor is kept for playback); the Diagnostics window says so. An edit of what a frame shows, a changed source file or a new version of the program simply makes those frames again; the final render never uses them.
  • Scrubbing a video in the media bin shows where you are. Moving the mouse over a video's card pages through it as before, and the card now writes the moment under the cursor — the file's own time, in the program's timecode — so "the take at about 1:40" can be found without placing the file first.
  • A heavy loop with Datamosh catches up in fewer laps on a graphics card. The card stood idle more than half the time while such a loop still showed "Loading": each piece of work waited for the card to be completely empty before the next was sent, and a frame whose Datamosh history was not ready yet was given up until the next lap even when the history arrived a moment later. Now the next piece is always waiting behind the one the card is drawing, and a frame is drawn as soon as its history is there.
  • Closing the program works while it is busy. Closed while a loop was still catching up — a Datamosh history being worked out, frames being prepared ahead — the program could keep its window frozen and never end, and you had to kill it. Now it first saves what must not be lost (your unsaved work goes to the recovery file as before), then stops its background work and ends within a few seconds whatever it was doing. The program's record of the session now says when you closed it and what the close waited for. A rare freeze-and-crash at the program's start, when a thumbnail arrived at the wrong moment, is gone too.
  • A render on a computer with a graphics card no longer crawls at real time. The card drew a simple frame in about a millisecond but took some fifty milliseconds to hand it back, and the render waited for every third frame to come back before drawing more, so even a plain region rendered no faster than it plays. The render now keeps as many frames on their way as the card needs to stay busy and passes each one on the moment it is back, with the same file as before.
  • The render's log is in the program's telemetry, not in a file of its own. Everything the render window's log says is in the telemetry journal and the trace you send, next to everything else that happened; render.log is no longer written, and Open log after a failed render opens the telemetry journal.
  • While you play, the preview works ahead instead of one frame at a time. The program used to draw each frame only when its moment came, and kept the graphics card waiting for every frame before starting the next, so on a computer with a graphics card the card stood idle most of the time while a heavy loop still showed "Loading" lap after lap. Now, while you play, it prepares the frames ahead of the one you see — the frame on screen first — keeps several of them on the card at once, as many as your card and memory have room for, and only shows frames that are finished. A heavy loop therefore plays without "Loading" from an earlier lap, and an ordinary piece plays ahead of itself too. Paused, scrubbing or jumping, the preview draws the frame you point at as before.
  • The colours of HD video now match other players. Footage from most cameras and phones is written in the HD colour standard (BT.709), but the program read every video as standard-definition, so reds and greens came out a little off — in the preview, the thumbnails and the render. It now reads the standard each file names, and for a file that names none it does what players do: HD as HD, smaller video as standard definition. Thumbnails and composition previews made with the old colours are made again once.
  • The render window says how long the render will take, and why it is slower than the preview. The preview usually draws a smaller picture than the file gets: the window now says so ("Preview 640×360 · render 1920×1080: 9.0× the pixels of a frame") and, once you have played the range, predicts the render time from what the preview's frames cost. On a computer without a graphics card the render also stops using more processor threads for drawing than help: it measures how fast the file is written and keeps only as many as make it faster, so a light stretch no longer renders slower than it should.
  • A loop with Datamosh stops waiting for work the graphics card already finished. Several kinds of background work — the moments a loop prepares ahead, effect previews, the Datamosh history — waited for everything the card had been given, by anyone, before taking their own result; and work ready to go to the card waited for an earlier piece of other work to finish even when other work had already made room. Now each waits only for its own result and sees room the moment it comes, so the card stands idle less while the loop still shows "Loading", and the picture on screen is shown as soon as it is drawn.
  • A densely cut project decodes less footage. When an edit keeps returning to the same file — a picture-in-picture of the footage under it, a backdrop, quick cuts between parts of one clip — the program used to send one reader back and forth between those places and decode the same stretch again and again. Each place now keeps a reader of its own (more of them for smaller videos), so the preview and the render decode about a sixth less on such an edit, with the same picture. Most of what is still decoded is the footage's own structure: a cut that starts between two keyframes has to be decoded from the keyframe before it.
  • A loop catches up in fewer laps on a computer with a graphics card. While a loop plays, the program works out in the background the moments it has not shown yet, so later laps play without work; it used to do that one moment at a time and waited for the frame on screen to finish before starting each, so the card and the processor mostly stood idle while the loop still showed "Loading". Now it works out several moments at once — as many as your computer has room for — and no longer waits for the frame on screen, which the card still draws first. On computers without a graphics card nothing changes: there the frame on screen and the background work share the processor, and doing more at once only made both slower.
  • The render window now offers the settings of a real export. Besides MP4 you can write MOV, MKV or WebM, and besides H.264 the video can be H.265, AV1, VP9 or ProRes 422 HQ; the rate is a constant quality, an average with a maximum, or a constant bitrate; the encoder speed, the keyframe interval, B-frames, 8- or 10-bit, the colour standard and range, the frame rate, a custom frame size, the sound as AAC, PCM, FLAC, Opus or none, and a title and comment are all yours to set. The window shows what will be rendered (the region or the whole project) and how big the file will be where that can be known. What your FFmpeg or the chosen container cannot do is shown greyed with the reason. Your settings are remembered for the next render, and you can save them as presets that are kept between projects; kt-cli export takes the same settings. The files now also say which colour standard they use, so players no longer guess it and shift the colours.
  • A finished render now says where its time went. The program's load report gets one line per render: how many frames, at what size, how much faster or slower than real time, and which work took the time (reading the footage, the graphics device, writing the file). The render preview in the editor usually shows a smaller picture than the file gets — a third of the size draws a ninth of the pixels — so a render slower than the preview is not always a fault; this line tells which it is.
  • On computers without Vulkan the program no longer closes when the graphics work stalls. With the OpenGL fallback, a preview frame or an effect's preparation held up by a busy disk or system for a few seconds could end the program with "Could not lock adapter context"; now the preview draws on a device of its own there, so such a stall costs a few preview frames while the rest of the window keeps working.
  • The program no longer closes when you maximize or resize its window while a loop plays. A double click on the window title during playback could end the program with a graphics error; now the window takes its new size a moment later and playback goes on. Any other graphics error is written to the log instead of closing the program.
  • Phaser, Compressor, Chorus, Flanger and Delay take noticeably less of the processor, with the same sound. Phaser and Compressor cost about a third and almost half less, Chorus, Flanger and Delay a fifth to a quarter less, VHS Tape's sound a tenth; Camera ISP with lens blur draws its first stage faster. Playback no longer takes memory from the system on every fraction of a second of sound, and the audio noise generator does a fraction of its former work. Every sound is the same to the last bit.
  • A project with a Datamosh plays its other pieces in real time again. Wherever the frame on screen had no Datamosh, the program worked out, before every look ahead, a walk of millions of frames for an effect that was not there — about 26 seconds each time on a fast computer — so the frames ahead were never prepared and the picture fell to a third of its speed. That walk is gone, so the pieces without Datamosh no longer slow down.
  • Datamosh works out its history faster and the frame you stopped on comes sooner. The broken stream's own state no longer goes back and forth between the graphics device and memory between its steps, and at large sizes it no longer encodes the same frames again on every frame; the frame on screen is worked out before the frames ahead of it.
  • A render of a project with a Datamosh uses the fast render path. Such a project used to be rendered one frame after another with the graphics device and the processor waiting for each other; now it decodes, draws and encodes at the same time like any other project, with the same result.
  • A long edit costs no more per frame than a short one, and typing a title in a big project no longer resolves every composition. Each preview frame, each prefetch and the composition strips used to look at every event of the project, so on a long edit the same frame cost more the longer the timeline was (on our heavy showcase grown to 41 000 events, 127 µs of planning per frame; now 1 µs, as on the short one). A keystroke in a title edited inside a composition used to work out every composition of the project on the interface's thread; now that happens in the background.
  • An effect in front of a Datamosh no longer makes each frame travel through the processor. With Camera ISP or another effect above Datamosh, every frame of its history was drawn on the graphics device, copied back into memory and copied again to the device that breaks the picture, with the history waiting for each copy; now the effect draws straight where Datamosh reads it, so that history catches up with less work and no waiting between the two.
  • A long loop keeps part of its work, whatever its length and whatever memory the computer has. The sound of a loop was kept in a fixed 64 MB, so a loop longer than about three minutes kept none of it and worked out every effect again on every lap; the decoded frames of a loop longer than the memory allowed were all decoded again every lap too. Now the kept sound takes the memory the loop needs, as far as the computer has it free, before anything else; and when a loop is still longer than what can be kept, the sound keeps the beginning of the loop and the frames keep a part, so each lap plays that part without work instead of none.
  • Play starts sooner after a pause. The program used to close the sound device a second after you stopped and open it again on every Play, which took tens of milliseconds and on a busy computer far longer; now it only quiets the device, which costs nothing while you are stopped, and Play wakes it at once. A click on the ruler followed by Play could also lose the first fraction of a second of sound on a busy computer and play it ahead of the picture; the first sound is now the material at the click.
  • A file that comes back, or a media file you point elsewhere, is heard at once. A section you had already played in a loop went on replaying the sound of the former file, and a file that was missing when the project opened never got its waveform after it came back. Now the new file's sound plays from the next moment, and the returned file's waveform is drawn.
  • The preview never shows half a picture. While a project's first frame was still loading, the preview showed whatever part of it was ready, with some clips missing and the effects laid over the rest; now its place stays empty under "Loading" until the whole frame is there, and the program no longer spends work drawing frames that are not ready and would be thrown away. The level meter under the cursor on a pause likewise no longer shows a level for sound that has not been read yet.
  • The load report is now part of the trace. The program no longer writes load-report.txt: the graphics cards it sees, which one drives your monitors, which one it chose and when the run started are written into its trace, with everything else it records. The button in Diagnostics that opened the load report now opens the trace folder — send that folder with a complaint. It stays on your computer until you send it.
  • Effect previews show the effect where it will really be. The pictures in the effect gallery (each variant, each preset, the strength drag) and in a morpher's gallery used to lay the effect over a plain still of the clip, so after a Datamosh they showed it over unbroken footage, and they skipped the clip's position, the track's effects and the composition around it; now each picture is the frame you will see after the click, worked out from the real project, and it reads "Loading" until it is ready instead of showing something else. Inside Datamosh, a masked effect placed in front of it now acts only inside its mask, a Pan 3D there follows its camera, and the track the vectors come from is read with its own effects; a Datamosh whose vectors come from a clip that starts earlier no longer crashes.
  • An effect placed in front of Datamosh now feeds it. With Camera ISP (or any effect) above Datamosh in an event's chain, Datamosh used to break the untouched footage and the effect was laid over the mosh afterwards; now the mosh breaks what that effect made, in the order you set, in the preview and in the export.
  • Your work is kept safe during long playback, and a long loop over a Datamosh keeps part of its work. The insurance copy of an edited project, meant to be written even while you play, used to wait for a pause, so a crash during a long playback lost every edit since it began; it is now written while the playback goes on. A loop over a Datamosh longer than the memory it may take used to work out its whole history again on every lap; it now keeps the part it can hold and only works out the rest, and it no longer asks memory for parts of the loop where the effect is not. Composition strips and project posters with a Datamosh no longer push the preview's work out of memory, and stop at once when you press Play.
  • A render never writes a frame without its layer because a file hiccupped, and its pictures no longer depend on what the preview tried. When a decoder failed to give a frame once, a render could write that frame without the clip, and say so in its log; now the render asks for the frame again and composes it again before writing it, and only a frame the file really does not have is still written without it and named. Effects like Color Grade, Posterize, Duotone and Vignette in a row are rendered the same way every time on the same computer, whatever the preview tried before, and a preview frame kept while the program was still measuring them is never shown in place of the finished one. On a computer whose graphics are busy with the frame on screen, background work no longer squeezes in front of every frame and makes the picture later still. Composition strips saved by earlier builds with empty title cells are drawn again once.
  • A Datamosh works out a loop ahead, and the graphics device is kept busy while you wait. A loop over a heavy Datamosh used to compute its history only a little ahead of the picture, so it took six or more laps before every frame was ready; now the program works the whole loop out from where you are to its end, while you play and also while you are paused inside the loop, at the lowest priority so the picture on screen still goes first (on our test loop most of the history is ready after two laps instead of five). The graphics device is no longer left waiting between the pieces of that work: the next piece is queued while one runs, the frame on screen is counted so the background work fits around it, and work it has never measured is planned from what it measured in earlier sessions. Loading a paused frame also converts decoded pictures on several processor cores.
  • Opening a project no longer freezes the window, and a loop on a slow computer stops being worked out lap after lap. Opening a large project used to hold the whole window while every file was examined and the engine prepared, for seconds on a heavy project; now the timeline appears at once, the menu answers, the preview says "Loading" until its picture is ready, and edits, Undo and Save work from the first moment. On a computer whose preview cannot keep up with every frame of a loop, each lap showed different frames and only those were kept, so the loop never stopped working; now the frames the preview skipped are prepared in the background, below the picture you are watching, and after a few laps the whole loop plays without work. An effect preview or a project poster being drawn no longer holds up the preview of a slow effect chain either.
  • Small things that the last changes left behind elsewhere. A composition holding a title or a generator showed empty frames in its strip on the timeline; it now shows them. A change of the bin's layout or the view made while Ctrl+S was still writing lost its unsaved mark, though it was not in the file; it now keeps it until the next save. Closing the window while playing could wait several seconds for the autosave and the poster, which stood paused behind the playback; they now run at once. A double click on the preview of a busy computer could both start playing and detach the window; it now only detaches. Several Backspace presses of the mask pen, and several ↓ ↑ in the search window, now each count when the program draws slowly.
  • Effects are never laid over a picture of another moment. While a Datamosh was still working out its history during playback, the preview showed an older picture of it and ran the effects after it — VHS Tape, Camera ISP, a track's or a composition's effects — over that old picture at the current moment, a frame that never exists, and the program even kept such frames. Now a frame is either the moment's own or not shown: the last full picture stays under "Loading — catching up: N", written where Loading always is, with how many frames of the history are left, playing or paused alike, and it goes as soon as the moment's own picture is ready. The same rule now holds for a slowed event in the "blend" frame mode whose neighbouring frame has not arrived yet, and for composition strips and project posters, which no longer keep a half-made frame; a poster of a project with a missing file shows the file's placeholder, as the preview does.
  • The decoded frames grow with your loop and your preview quality, and the numbers say what they count. The frames decoded for playing ahead were kept in a fixed 512 MB whatever the machine had, so a long or high-quality loop dropped and decoded its frames again on every lap, and choosing a higher preview quality changed nothing. Now they take the memory the loop and the look-ahead need at the quality you chose, as far as the computer has it free, and give it back at once when you render. The status bar's "cache: 39/535 MB" was the audio and the video caches, not used and limit: it now reads "frames: held/bound MB" and "memory: MB" — all the program holds — and Diagnostics shows what that memory is made of, the caches and the rest (decoders, the graphics driver, the interface).
  • A short loop with effects sounds the same on every lap, from the first. A loop over a reverb, a Slowed or a VHS Tape whose first part you had already heard could have its following laps recorded with a wrong start — the effects began again as if after a jump instead of ringing the lap before — and that lap was then repeated every time round. Now the program carries the effects on through what it replays before it renders anything new, so every lap is what continuous playback gives, and a moment where a file was not ready in time is no longer kept with its gap ringing in the effects. A jump also no longer carries the old place into a ducking compressor's key, and a jump inside a composition whose track has an echo plays the echo.
  • A paused program no longer keeps the sound card busy. The sound device used to stay open the whole time and was woken dozens of times a second on a pause just to play silence. It now opens when you press Play and closes a second after you stop, so a pause wakes nothing; if the device cannot be opened, the notice bell says why.
  • A Datamosh works out its history in batches on the graphics device, and a jump back costs a few frames, not the whole history. The effect used to compute its history one frame at a time, waiting for the graphics device twice per frame — on a graphics card most of that time was the wait, not the work, and the preview crept along with little processor load. Now up to 32 frames go to the device at once and only the pictures you will see come back; a frame of the history you jumped away from is found again from a nearby checkpoint (at most 16 frames to recompute instead of hundreds). The picture is exactly the same as before.
  • A loop is kept whole as far as the computer's memory allows. The finished pictures of a loop you have played were kept in a fixed 512 MB — about ten seconds at preview size and one second at full HD — so a longer loop, like a heavy Datamosh region, went on being worked out lap after lap however much memory was free, and a loop just a little too long reused nothing at all. Now the program measures the memory it may take while it runs (a limit set for it included) and keeps every frame of the loop within half of it; after a few laps the loop plays with nothing left to compute. A loop too long for the memory keeps part of itself instead of none, a render takes that memory back while it runs and holds no pictures it has already used, and the Diagnostics window shows where the memory went.
  • A heavy effect working in the background no longer holds up the picture you are watching. Rendering, effect previews, posters and the look-ahead of a Datamosh used to send the graphics card long batches of work, and the frame you were looking at waited behind them — on a card that runs the window and the effects together, up to most of a second. Now the card is given the frame on screen first and the rest in short pieces between frames: with a render and a Datamosh working beside the preview, its frames wait at most a few tens of milliseconds (a computer without a graphics card: the worst wait 764 ms → 73 ms, three times as many frames shown). A Datamosh you have moved away from stops working out its history at once, and a paused render no longer wakes up to check whether you resumed.
  • A Datamosh costs the processor a fraction of what it did, and a loop over it stops recomputing it. Every frame of a Datamosh used to work its whole schedule out again — and the program asked that dozens of times a second while looking ahead — and converted every picture's colours on the processor; now the schedule is worked out once per change and the conversion runs on the graphics device, so the effect's own share of a frame fell to about a third (on a 720-line Datamosh: 10–17 → 4.4 ms of processor a frame) and it moves a third of the data it did. A loop over a long Datamosh no longer forgets its history on every lap: the program keeps as much of it as the loop needs and the computer's memory allows, so from the second lap the effect itself costs nothing. The picture and the sound are exactly the same as before.
  • Saving and bringing in files no longer freeze the window, and background work steps aside while you play. Ctrl+S used to stand on the disk for seconds on a busy computer, and dropping a file onto the timeline, placing one from the bin or undoing its arrival opened files with the window waiting; now they happen in the background and the window answers at once. While you play, filmstrip thumbnails, effect previews, composition strips, project posters, loudness analysis and waveform building wait, so playback has the computer to itself, and they finish as soon as you stop. A wide filmstrip or effects gallery no longer redraws its own pictures over and over, and a program standing still no longer wakes up a few times a second to check on things.
  • Colour effects in a row cost about as much as one. Color Grade, Posterize, Duotone and Vignette placed one after another on an event or a track used to pass the whole picture through the graphics device once each; now they run together in one pass, so a chain of four or six of them takes about a quarter or a sixth of the device's time it did (six at full HD on a computer without a graphics card: 9.3 ms → 2.2 ms a frame). The picture is exactly the same as before.
  • Quick keys and double clicks are no longer lost on a busy computer. When the program drew slowly (a build running beside it, a computer without a graphics card), several keys pressed quickly could count as one: → → → ← moved the cursor nowhere, two Ctrl+Z undid one edit, two quick taps of Space paused instead of stopping at the start, a short tap could do nothing at all, and a double click could open nothing. Now every key runs as pressed, a tap stays a tap, and the double press and the double click allow for how long the program takes to draw a frame.
  • The program rests again right after an edit. After a change, while it checked which played frames it can still show without work, the window redrew itself as fast as it could — on a busy computer for seconds, taking several processor cores while nothing moved. It now redraws only when the check has something to show.
  • Playback no longer stutters at its very start on a busy computer. The first moment of sound after Play or a jump could break up while another program loaded the processor; the start now waits until its sound is ready, as it already did for the first frame.
  • A loop you have played no longer shows "Loading" again. A short loop under a heavy chain with Datamosh (Camera ISP → Datamosh → VHS Tape) could show "Loading" lap after lap, and pausing on one of its frames waited seconds for the effect's history again, however many times you had played it. Now a frame you have seen is shown straight from what was kept, without decoding or working the effect out again: the loop settles within a few laps, pausing inside it shows the picture at once, and the same holds at a slow rate and when you scrub back over it.
  • The program now keeps a trace a developer can ask questions of. Beside the journal, the data folder holds trace/: a compact record of what every part of the program did and why — which frame waited for what, what the cache kept or dropped, what the effects computed, what the machine and its graphics card are. Send the folder with a report and the question "why was it Loading here" is answered from your own run, with no test build and no repeating it on another machine. It costs nothing while the program stands still and is never sent anywhere.
  • Dragging a slider on a big project no longer stalls the program. Every change, and every step of a slider drag in an effects window, rebuilt the whole sound and video engine four or five times over, partly while the window waited: on a project of two thousand events each step held the interface for about a tenth of a second, and a drag kept two and a half processor cores busy. Now each change is prepared once, in the background, and only the event you touched is worked out again; the window answers at once, the sound plays on, and changing the loop region costs nothing at all.
  • The first frame of an effect no longer stalls. Opening a project, adding an effect or seeking to a Datamosh or a generator used to freeze the picture for a moment — up to several seconds for Camera ISP or VHS Tape on a computer without a graphics card — while the effect was prepared for the graphics device. The program now prepares the effects a project uses in the background as soon as it opens or an effect is added, the window no longer stands still while the video engine starts, and on a graphics card that can keep them the prepared effects are remembered for the next start.
  • Modulation effects no longer get heavier with a detailed frequency curve. Tremolo, Auto-Pan, Vibrato, Chorus, Flanger and Phaser re-read their whole frequency curve for every sample, so a formula on the frequency (which becomes a point per frame) made a minute-long event cost ten times the processor; now the cost does not depend on the curve. Formulas on curves are also worked out much faster everywhere, and a change on a project with shaped speed curves recomputes only the curves it touched. Everything sounds and looks exactly as before.
  • An edit on a project with shaped speed curves is fast again. A speed curve with a smooth or formula segment made every change rebuild the sound engine in about half a second on a big project (the work grew with the square of the curve's length); now that rebuild takes a few milliseconds. Many transitions, a composition placed many times, a morpher layer over many events and chains of linked curves no longer make edits or opening slower out of proportion either.
  • A crash now says where it happened. When the program is ended by a fault in a graphics driver, a decoder or its own code, the crash window names the part of the program that faulted and what it was doing, lists what you and the program did in the last moments, and the report in the log folder holds the whole trail with file and line, ready to send. A command-line render that crashes prints the same report.
  • Rendering from the command line works with no screen attached. kt-cli export on a machine with no display (a server, a terminal session) crashed at once; it renders now. The editor also no longer reloads every graphics driver each time the load report is written.
  • A heavy effect no longer freezes the program. When an effect takes seconds to draw a frame (a Datamosh with an extreme setting, say), the picture comes late, but the windows, the timeline, playback and Ctrl+Z answer at once: you can always undo the effect that made it slow. If a moment of the interface still stands, the journal now says which part of the window it stood in.
  • A Datamosh no longer stalls the picture. After you added or changed a Datamosh, the program could ask for the same frames over and over, throw each one away before using it, and leave a paused frame or a short loop standing still for as long as you watched, with the interface freezing for seconds at a time. Now its frames are fetched in the order the effect uses them, the effect is worked out in the background, and the interface never waits for it: a loop over a Datamosh plays, and on a computer too slow for the effect in real time you see it run late rather than not at all.
  • Camera ISP and Datamosh ask less of the graphics card. The camera simulation no longer recomputes the same sensor row and column for every pixel around it, and Datamosh's encoder spreads its work over the whole card instead of a few of its lanes and sends a quarter of the data. They look exactly as before.
  • The program now writes down what the graphics card spent its time on. Every busy second, the telemetry journal (and load-report.txt) gets a line with the card's name, the frame size, how many milliseconds a frame took on the card and which effect pass took them — VHS Tape's head read, Camera ISP's demosaic, the composite. Diagnostics shows the same line while it plays. Nothing to switch on and nothing to measure by hand: a normal run is enough.
  • A range you have played plays again for free. The picture after the effects and the sound after the effects are kept as you first saw and heard them, like a prerender: a loop over heavy effects (VHS, Camera ISP, a slowed composition) runs at the project's frame rate from its third lap, with no decoding and no effect running. Changing a parameter recomputes only the part it touches. The strips at the top of the timeline and under each event are now bright where a range plays without work and keep their darker colour where only its sources are ready.
  • Editing during playback no longer cuts the sound. On a large project every change used to stop the sound for a moment.
  • A composition placed many times no longer eats the memory. Its inner effects are prepared only for the places that are playing.
  • One journal of what happened and what you did, with the time. The program now keeps telemetry-journal.log in its data folder: every busy second, each playback with its frame rate and dropouts, the warnings, and your own actions (an edit by name, a window opened, play and pause, a save) — each written the moment it happens, with the clock time, and kept after a crash. Press Ctrl+Alt+M or Mark the moment in Diagnostics (with a note if you like) when something goes wrong, and the line says “here”. Diagnostics shows the journal at the bottom whatever the window's height, and load-report.txt is now its last quarter of an hour with real times instead of “seconds ago”. Nothing in it is ever sent anywhere.
  • Sound effects take less of the processor. VHS Tape's sound costs less than half of what it did, and Gate, Limiter, Distortion and Bitcrusher a tenth: they no longer redo the same calculation on every sample while their knobs stand still, and on a processor with AVX2 every sound effect runs on its wider instructions. They sound exactly as before, to the last bit.
  • An open effects window no longer works while you only move the mouse. A number sitting exactly at the end of its range (VHS Tape's dark clip at its floor, Slowed+Reverb or Camera ISP at a ceiling) was taken as an edit on every move, and each one rebuilt the whole sound and picture engine: on a big project two processor cores ran flat out. Now only what you change is an edit, and the load report says when a busy thread did work it does not count instead of calling it rest.
  • The mouse over a big project costs a fraction of what it did. Moving it over the preview, along the timeline or over an open effects window no longer makes the program redo work for every event of the project: a frame now costs what is on screen, at any scroll and zoom, and playback leaves the picture more of the processor. Diagnostics › Performance shows what one interface frame costs and where ("UI frame … ms").
  • A pause is a pause. A program standing still does no work now: with several releases of a composition on the timeline it kept rendering their previews in a circle, and every move of the mouse started another one. Moving the mouse no longer costs anything that depends on what the timeline shows, and each release keeps its preview between openings.
  • Effects run on the card your monitor is plugged into. On a desktop they could end up on the processor's built-in graphics.
  • The load report. If the program holds the processor for more than a few seconds it writes load-report.txt in its data folder by itself: which threads, which work, which graphics devices. Diagnostics shows the same live, with a button that opens the folder. The file stays on your computer.
  • Work the way your hands already know. At the first start, or in File › Preferences…, choose a Layout & Controls style: ours, like Vegas, or like Premiere Pro, DaVinci Resolve, Final Cut Pro or After Effects. The keys, the wheel and the panels change at once, and each tile says what that program has and we do not. Customize changes any key, and the settings code under the tiles brings it all back after a reinstall.
  • Renders with no graphics card are faster, most of all under the VHS simulation and on events with a camera, and the preview gains the same in those places.
  • A render no longer stalls on a file cut short. A file whose header promises more than it holds is now read to its real end once, and the render goes on with the last picture.
  • Every picture is now made by one engine, on the graphics card. The separate processor path is gone, so the preview and the render can no longer disagree, and effects no longer exist twice. With no graphics card the program runs the same engine through Vulkan on the processor, and a render there uses several devices at once, as many as the memory allows. A computer with no Vulkan, DX12 or Metal driver has no picture and no render, and the program says so: on Linux install mesa-vulkan-drivers, on Windows a graphics driver.
  • Shapes, gradients and the countdown generate up to fifty times faster. Rectangles, ellipses, lines, gradients, corners, noise and the leader now draw as shaders.
  • Slowed footage in blending mode no longer shows a frame of the wrong weight.
  • A render takes much less memory. A dense 1080p edit went from 17 GB to under 9 and got faster, and on a machine short of memory the render gives up speed instead of being killed: the same edit finished under a limit of 3 GB.
  • A render comes out the same every time. Rendering a busy edit could quietly drop a layer from a few frames, different ones on each run, leaving wrong pictures in the file. Now every frame keeps all its layers, and the speed of the render is unchanged. If a source really cannot give a picture, the render's log says which file and at what time, and opens by itself so you see it.
  • A picture in the project no longer holds up the waveforms. One still kept a processor core busy for hours and grew the memory, and the waveforms of the files after it never came.
  • Ctrl+S during a freeze no longer cuts the event. If the interface stalled for a moment and Ctrl was already released when it woke, the program saw a plain S and split the event under the playhead.
  • A failed render explains itself better. The message no longer starts with a technical "io:", and the window says no encoder opened instead of still claiming to choose one.
  • The timeline stops fighting the hand. A bottom corner of an event always changes its length. On a low row or a short event a press moves it instead of touching the volume, and the level is in the right-click menu. The sound of an event goes down to mute, and the event now says its level right after the name: −12 dB, 40 %, mute.
  • The space bar does more. Held from a pause it plays only while held and stops where the picture got to. Ctrl+Space plays backward. The speed builds up smoothly and comes back faster. A short press and two quick presses work as before.
  • Step one frame with ← and →, or Ctrl+click on Back and Forward.
  • Freeze frame. Right-click an event and choose "Insert frame hold (freeze frame)": the picture stands for 2 seconds at the playhead and goes on from the same frame. The event keeps its length.
  • Tracks can be dragged again by their header, which had stopped working long ago. The header also shows a hand now, and a click on its free part is the strongest jump to the left.
  • Jumps and scrolling. A click at the timeline's edge jumps even over an event, and no longer opens it. The side scrollbar can be caught without resizing the window. Zooming the rows keeps the track under the mouse. The end of a range marker can be moved. Empty morpher and camera rows carry no captions. When playback freezes, the bell says where.
  • Datamosh encodes on the graphics card. The effect's codec now runs as a shader, and even with no card, through Vulkan on the processor, a frame takes about a third less time. Existing moshes may look slightly different, because the search picks some other vectors.
  • Hardware encoding on Linux no longer risks the render. Choosing h264_vaapi used to end the program. Now the render tries a hardware encoder on the side first: if the graphics driver fails or crashes there, a render left on Auto goes on with the next encoder, and one you chose by hand stops with a message saying what went wrong, while the program and your project stay open. On Intel and AMD graphics the render can now use the card, though we have not yet been able to test that on real hardware.
  • Camera ISP records the sound too. On an event with linked audio, the sound goes through the device's microphone: the phone's port and noise suppressor, a webcam's 16 kHz, a security camera's G.711 and wind, with an automatic gain control that lifts the room between words. The looks set it, and the Microphone block in the panel lets you change every step. A project that uses a look with a device microphone, or changes a device's sound settings, opens only in this version and newer.
  • Datamosh breaks the sound too. On an event with linked audio, the sound now goes through a real audio codec in the same stream: where the picture loses a keyframe the sound loses a packet at the same moment and smears until the next clean keyframe — a Reset key heals both.
  • VHS Tape now plays the sound too. Put it on an event with linked audio and the audio gets the same deck: Hi-Fi tracks that crackle exactly where a clogged head or a dropout breaks the picture, or the linear track — dull at LP, with tape hiss and the capstan's wobble. Its Sound section is in the deck panel; the checkbox in the audio's chain switches it off.
  • The preview keeps up at full quality. A shot over its own blurred backdrop used to make the program decode the same video about ten times over; now each picture is decoded once, the sound no longer drops out there, and playback at the project's full size stays smooth where it used to stutter. The interface stays responsive during playback, even on a computer without a graphics card, where frames are now prepared ahead on several processor cores, and a cut into a large 4K file no longer arrives late. The first play after opening a project starts with its sound instead of a moment of silence.
  • A busy disk no longer makes the program forget its previews. On a spinning disk under heavy writing, opening a project could rebuild the previews of its compositions, and the waveforms and loudness of its media, as if seen for the first time. The program now keeps using what it stored.
  • The final render is several times faster, and it no longer crashes on some footage. It used one core for everything in turn; now it reads, draws, converts and encodes at the same time on all of them, and the sound renders alongside the picture instead of after it. A project that jumps around in long 4K files no longer reads minutes of video it does not show, and a picture-in-picture of the same clip no longer makes it re-read the clip for every frame. The render of a project with a square 1080×1080 video used to crash within seconds. On a machine without a graphics card the render now draws on the processor's cores, which is the faster way there.
  • Camera ISP no longer smears the edges of the frame. "Phone at night" and the looks with a distorting lens filled a band along the edges — about 30 px on a 1080p frame — with streaks of the edge pixels. The simulated lens is now framed on what your footage recorded, and the camera's processor crops its distortion correction to what its sensor saw, as a phone does: the edges are picture, and a corrected lens frames slightly tighter.
  • Pitch: choose what happens to the echo before it. When a reverb or an echo stands before a pitch (Slowed+Reverb under a morpher's pitch, for example), the pitch effect now has the line "Echo of the effects before the pitch": cut at the event's end (as before — the joins stay seamless) or rings on after the event (the echo goes on past the event's end, pitched, as without the pitch). Projects that use "rings on" open only in this version and newer.
  • A loop over an echo before a pitch no longer dips at every lap. When the loop region started at an event with an echo or reverb before its pitch, each pass began with a short hole (with "rings on") or a sudden drop with a bit of foreign sound (with "cut"). Every pass now starts as playing from that point does, and the echo of the pass before still rings on over it.
  • Playing layered 4K footage keeps its frames ready. Where several layers play at once — a shot over its blurred backdrop, a picture-in-picture, a composition — the preview used to ask for more frames ahead than its memory holds and threw away the ones it needed next, so the picture stalled and Diagnostics filled with "dropped before the first read". The look-ahead now fits the memory, and frames the playhead has already passed are no longer decoded.
  • Ctrl+F shows what it finds again. The search window kept the height of its empty field, so the media, events and markers it found were hidden under its bottom edge until you dragged the window larger.
  • Opening a project with a reel no longer asks to save changes you did not make. Once the reel's preview had drawn on the timeline, opening another project or quitting asked "save your changes?" about a project nobody had touched, and quitting left a recovery file behind.
  • Rendering a region no longer closes the program at 100 %. A render of a region that does not start exactly on a frame — any region drawn by hand, even 0.2 s — used to reach 100 % and take the whole program down, sometimes with the file half-written. It now finishes, shows its summary and closes like any other.
  • A camera you can film your frame with: Camera ISP. The new effect undoes the camera that made your footage back into a scene, then films it again with a simulated camera: a lens (defocus, distortion, chromatic aberration, vignetting, colour shading), a colour mosaic (RGGB and its phases, Quad Bayer, X-Trans, RGBW, RGB-IR with infrared pixels), a sensor that counts electrons with their real noise, blooming and banding, and the camera's processor with a block for every one of those defects — black level, row/column correction, defect pixels, green balance, raw denoise, lens shading, white balance, demosaic, distortion and colour-fringe correction, colour matrix, tone curve, denoise, sharpening and YUV with 4:2:0. Every block can be switched off or set wrong, "View" shows the picture after any stage, and the looks follow from it: "Phone at night", "Cheap webcam", "Security cam, IR", "Cinema raw", "Wrong CFA phase", "No IR-cut filter". The noise is the same on every play and render.
  • A real start window. The welcome window has three columns — Start (the tour, templates drawn in their frame's shape, the five lessons with your progress), Recent (your projects with their pictures, as many per row as fit) and What's new, now readable in its own column. Each column scrolls on its own, and the window can be made as large as the screen.
  • File → Preferences… holds the program's settings. Language, Economy UI, whether the welcome window opens at start, the usage statistics, the daily update check and FFmpeg are in one window, each switch in one place; the View menu keeps only what changes the view.
  • The language you chose stays chosen. Opening another project used to forget it, and the next start came up in the system language; Economy UI was forgotten the same way.
  • A real VHS: the tape is written and read back. The new VHS Tape effect does not paint stripes on the picture — it records it as a VHS deck does (the brightness on an FM carrier, the colour on a low "colour-under" carrier, two heads on a spinning drum writing slanted tracks) and plays the tape back. Snow, colour smear, the noise bar, the tear at the bottom and wobbly lines come out of the causes: click a head on the drawn drum and make it dirty, clogged or chipped, turn the tracking, switch SP/LP, a TBC, four heads for a clean pause, or record on one deck and play on another. The old VHS look is still there.
  • Datamosh — a real one. The new Datamosh effect runs its own little video codec over the clip — motion search, a prediction loop, quantised detail, keyframes — and lets you break it on purpose: drop the keyframes so the previous shot gets dragged by the new shot's motion, repeat one frame's motion until it blooms, freeze the reference, scale, turn or swap the motion vectors, borrow the motion of the clip on the track above or below, lose detail or whole blocks. The breakages take curves: switch the mosh on and off, or put a Reset key on the beat to start clean from that frame. Presets: Cut mosh, Bloom, Transplant, Melt. Any frame looks the same when you play up to it, jump to it or render it.
  • Masks. Right-click the picture → Mask → Rectangle, Ellipse or Pen, and draw right over the preview: the pen makes a Bézier path (click — a corner, click and pull — a smooth point). Each mask has feather (smooth or linear), expansion, opacity, invert and a mode — add, subtract, intersect, difference — and several masks combine from the top down. A mask on the event's picture follows the event when you move, scale or rotate it; an effect can be limited to its own masks (under its parameters in the effects window) — a blur on a face, a colour only in a corner; a track can be masked from its window. The stopwatch on a mask animates its whole shape: drag a point at another moment and the shape is keyed there.
  • Composition previews no longer get rebuilt by chance when a project opens. Opening a project sometimes found its own index file "busy" and drew the frames and waveform of every composition all over again; now the saved previews come back every time.
  • Diagnostics holds all of Performance, with three graphs. The Performance box no longer sits under the media bin — the bin gets the whole column. The gauge button (or View → Diagnostics…) opens one window with every number the box had and three graphs side by side in time: playback, FFmpeg activity and the cache. Make the window larger and the graphs grow.
  • Sound generators: tone, noise, sweep, beeps and silence. Edit → Create a generator → Audio puts a line-up tone, white/pink/brown noise, a sine sweep, a train of sync beeps or a stretch of silence on an audio track. Levels are in dBFS (−20 dBFS of tone and of noise read the same on the meters), a tone or a beep can go to one channel, and the sound is the same on every play, seek and render.
  • "Create a generator" left the File menu. It is in Edit now, and in a track's right-click menu, which puts the generator exactly where you clicked — a video track offers the picture kinds, an audio track the sound kinds. The media bin keeps its item.
  • Every window can be made bigger, and what is inside grows with it. Drag a window's corner: the effects chain, the curve graph, the lists, the Guide and the render log take the new room instead of leaving an empty frame around a small box. Each window remembers the size you gave it — an effects window opens as large as the last one you enlarged.
  • The Guide reads like a manual. Its tables are real tables, with a shaded header, lines between the cells and a key column as wide as its keys; every "I want to…" entry is its own card, the place to act written under it.
  • Adding an effect shows one big gallery. The "+ effect" picker is as wide as its window and as tall as the screen allows — presets first, then the effects — with more thumbnails per row in a wider window.
  • No button is cut off at the end of the toolbar. In a narrow window the buttons that do not fit (Render, Search, Diagnostics, Save…) move into a ⋯ menu at the end of the row.
  • Zigzag and the other segment shapes on one piece of a curve, or on a hundred. Right-click a segment, or Ctrl+click several, or drag across empty space in the curve graph: under "Shape of all segments" a row appears with the same fields for just those segments. Values that differ show "—"; a typed number sets all of them, dragging the field shifts each by the same amount.
  • Windows: the welcome window names your project folders plainly — C:\Users\…, not \\?\C:\Users\….
  • A project sounds and looks the same on Windows and Linux. Slowed+Reverb, the phaser and pitch shift gave slightly different bytes on Windows; every effect now uses the program's own math, so a render is identical on both — and on any processor.
  • Forcing an encoder this computer does not have (VAAPI on Windows) now says so by name instead of an empty error.
  • If Kinetren crashes, a window says so at once — the error, the version and the last lines of the log, with Restore the project and Open the log folder. Before, you learnt it only at the next start, if at all.
  • Restoring after a crash brings back your own footage. The restored project no longer plays a lesson's test patterns in place of your sources, and keeps its own name.
  • Rendering a region that does not start on a frame no longer closes the program.
  • The log keeps one file per run (the four previous runs next to it), each starting with the version and the start time in your time zone.
  • The tour points where to act. Every lesson step outlines its place — the menu item, the event, the marker, the button in a window — and Show scrolls to it or opens its menu instead of doing the step for you. Keys and buttons in the lesson text are drawn as keycaps.
  • The tour no longer lags or misleads. "Play a part in a loop" counts the moment the loop is on, even with a window open; the transitions lesson teaches Transition with previous (an overlap stays a cut); after an effect or a transition the lesson says what changed and moves the playhead to where you can see it. "Next lesson" no longer asks to save the lesson's own copy, the lessons panel no longer hides the right end of the toolbar, and the render lesson tells silly jokes while it waits.
  • Click a marker on the ruler to put the playhead on it.
  • Pitch no longer tears between short events. Cut an event with pitch into many short pieces and they sound exactly like the uncut event; any pitched event starts and ends without a dip — also when the pitch comes after Slowed+Reverb or an echo, or from a morpher.
  • Changing an audio effect takes effect at once. Put a filter where an equaliser stood and you hear the filter right away — before, the old effect kept playing with the new settings until you jumped in time.
  • The strength slider in the effects gallery no longer mixes the settings of two different effects.
  • Every effect, transition and generator is now a plugin inside — blur, glow, VHS, noise, the chroma key and the rest moved too. Your projects open and look exactly as before.

kt26.10

  • Windows. A portable Windows build; FFmpeg is found on the computer or downloaded with one click.
  • FFmpeg 9 works, as do 6, 7 and 8.
  • Under wine the interface is dark everywhere and our own title row is back.
  • A quiet reminder about updates. Once a day the program checks whether a newer release is out and says so in the bell — no pop-ups.
  • A welcome window at start. New projects from templates, the recent projects with a frame of each, the tour and this page. One tile is highlighted: Enter takes it. Switch the window off with Show at start; Help → Welcome window… brings it back.
  • The tour. Short lessons on a demo project made of generators. A step closes by itself when the project shows it done — see Getting started.
  • Help → Guide… finds where a thing is done: type what you want, or open a page of this guide.
  • One window shell. Every window closes by its cross and by Esc, the top one first, and no window grows by itself.
  • The render window names the encoder before the first frame, counts the bytes and asks before replacing a file.
  • The FFmpeg window tells what it downloads, where it goes, how fast, and why.
  • Effects are plugins inside. The built-in effects moved into their own crates behind one interface; projects keep their bytes.
  • Faster event grids. A grid computes one cell and copies it; a morpher layer at strength zero costs nothing.
